statement: In adults with alcohol use disorder in double-blind outpatient trials of 12 to 52 weeks, mostly with a psychosocial co-intervention, other medicines compared with placebo, as pooled in a 2023 review for the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (McPheeters et al., 2023; funded by the agency; no conflicts declared): topiramate is associated with fewer drinking days (−7.2 percentage points, 95% CI −14.3 to −0.1; 8 trials, 1,080 people), fewer heavy-drinking days (−6.2, −10.9 to −1.4; 9 trials) and about 2 fewer drinks on drinking days (−2.0, −3.1 to −1.0; 7 trials), each graded moderate strength of evidence by the review, with more tingling (risk ratio 3.08, 2.11 to 4.49), changes in taste (3.01, 1.70 to 5.34) and problems with thinking (2.37, 1.58 to 3.55); baclofen with fewer people returning to any drinking (risk ratio 0.83, 0.70 to 0.98; 8 trials) and gabapentin with fewer returning to heavy drinking (0.90, 0.82 to 0.98; 3 trials), both graded low, with more drowsiness, sleepiness or dizziness and, with gabapentin, problems with thinking (2.76, 1.51 to 5.06). Disulfiram did not reduce return to any drinking in blinded trials (risk ratio 1.03, 0.90 to 1.17; 3 trials; low), although no trial tested taking it under supervision, which the earlier review says may underestimate its benefit (Jonas et al., 2014). A long-acting injection of naltrexone showed no clear difference in return to any or heavy drinking (2 trials each; low). In the earlier review, nalmefene was associated with 2 fewer heavy-drinking days a month (−2.0, −3.0 to −1.0; 2 trials), and about 1 more person in 12 stopped a trial because of side effects (number needed to harm 12, 7 to 50). Deaths were too few to judge (8 with baclofen against 3 with placebo in 4 trials). The 2023 review updates the 2014 one and shares most of its trials, and it reports results only for medicines with at least low strength of evidence for benefit. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: Several other medicines have been compared with dummy pills. Topiramate was linked to fewer drinking days (about 7 fewer in every 100) and about 2 fewer drinks on drinking days, but tingling, changes in taste and trouble thinking were more common. Baclofen and gabapentin were linked to small benefits, but the evidence is weak. In blinded trials, disulfiram did not reduce drinking; no trial tested taking it with someone watching. A long-acting naltrexone injection showed no clear effect on going back to drinking. Most of these medicines were tested in only a few trials.
population: Adults with alcohol use disorder (mostly alcohol dependence) in double-blind outpatient trials of 12 to 52 weeks, mostly with a psychosocial co-intervention; mostly White men in their 40s
exposure: Topiramate, baclofen, gabapentin, disulfiram, injectable naltrexone and nalmefene, as given in the trials
outcome: Drinking days, heavy-drinking days, drinks per drinking day, return to any or heavy drinking; side effects and stopping a trial because of them; deaths
magnitude: McPheeters et al. 2023, against placebo: topiramate, percentage of drinking days WMD −7.2 (−14.3 to −0.1), 8 trials, 1080; heavy drinking days −6.2 (−10.9 to −1.4), 9 trials, 1210; drinks per drinking day −2.0 (−3.1 to −1.0), 7 trials, 922; all moderate; paraesthesia RR 3.08 (2.11 to 4.49), taste abnormalities 3.01 (1.70 to 5.34), cognitive dysfunction 2.37 (1.58 to 3.55). Baclofen, return to any drinking RR 0.83 (0.70 to 0.98), 8 trials, 995, low; drowsiness 1.46 (1.15 to 1.86), dizziness 1.89 (1.40 to 2.55), sleepiness 1.81 (1.11 to 2.97); deaths 8 against 3 (4 trials, 660), insufficient. Gabapentin, return to heavy drinking 0.90 (0.82 to 0.98), return to any drinking 0.92 (0.83 to 1.02), 3 trials, 522, low; cognitive dysfunction 2.76 (1.51 to 5.06), dizziness 1.70 (1.24 to 2.32). Disulfiram, return to any drinking 1.03 (0.90 to 1.17), 3 trials, 622, low (no effect). Injectable naltrexone, return to any drinking 0.96 (0.90 to 1.03), 2 trials, 939; return to heavy drinking 1.00 (0.82 to 1.21), 2 trials, 615; low (no effect). Jonas et al. 2014: nalmefene, heavy drinking days per month WMD −2.0 (−3.0 to −1.0), 2 trials, 806; drinks per drinking day −1.02 (−1.77 to −0.28), 3 trials, 608; withdrawal from trials because of adverse events NNH 12 (7 to 50), 5 trials, 2054.

Baclofen, return to any drinking RR 0.83 (0.70 to 0.98), 8 trials, 995, low (imprecision and inconsistency), with no effect on other outcomes. Gabapentin, return to any drinking 0.92 (0.83 to 1.02) and return to heavy drinking 0.90 (0.82 to 0.98), 3 trials, 522, low. Results are presented only for medicines with at least low strength of evidence for benefit; ondansetron, varenicline and prazosin had low or insufficient evidence and are not reported in the article.

evidence.extracted: Well-controlled trials of disulfiram did not show overall reductions in alcohol consumption; in a subgroup of the largest trial, fewer drinking days were found for participants who returned to drinking and had a complete set of assessments. None of the disulfiram trials evaluated supervised administration, which the authors say may underestimate its benefit in supervised treatment programmes.

risk_of_bias.note: Per-trial risk of bias is not shown in the 2023 review, whose AMSTAR 2 rating is critically low; in 2014 most trials were rated medium risk of bias, and drinking was self-reported.

inconsistency.note: Not rated separately; the review downgraded baclofen for inconsistency, which the claim reports as the review's low grade.

indirectness.note: Worded for the trial populations; disulfiram's untested supervised use is stated.

imprecision.note: Most findings rest on 2 to 9 trials; the topiramate drinking-days interval reaches −0.1 points; the baclofen and gabapentin intervals reach close to no effect; the disulfiram null rests on 3 trials; deaths are too few to judge.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the 2023 review; with few trials per medicine it cannot be judged.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; rated down for risk of bias and imprecision, giving low for the claim as a whole; the review's own grades (moderate for topiramate's drinking outcomes, low for the others) are reported, not adopted. The claim gathers several medicines with different directions (topiramate, baclofen and gabapentin linked to less drinking; disulfiram and the injection to no clear difference), so it is worded as an association rather than a single effect. Overlap: the 2023 review updates the 2014 one, so the two are counted once. Status replicated: each finding rests on more than one trial in the same direction. Medicines for which the review reported nothing (ondansetron, varenicline, prazosin) are not claimed; no doses are given.
